title: When Auditing meets Telemetry: a practical example.
summary: A real case where Default Dimension records disappeared. Change Log showed the user and the time, but telemetry traces and page views showed that the user had unknowingly triggered the deletion by running a calculation action. A temporary-record check placed too late in the code caused real dimension data to be deleted. The fix was to move that check to the first line of the OnAfterDeleteEvent.
key_points: Change Log records what changed (user, date, deletion event) but not always why or the context of the action
Telemetry traces provide execution context showing which code triggered the deletion and when
The combination of both auditing tools solved a mystery where the user was innocent but the Change Log was factually correct
A late placement of a temporary record check caused real data deletion instead of temporary record deletion
Moving the temporary record validation to the start of the OnAfterDeleteEvent prevented accidental dimension deletion

quotes.text: Telemetry can do A LOT of good things but unfortunately it was not meant to be used for pure AUDITING purposes.
quotes.why_it_matters: Clarifies the intended scope of telemetry and sets expectations for when to use Change Log instead

quotes.text: With a simple query that scanned both traces and page views, we were able to determine the innocence of the user
quotes.why_it_matters: Shows how telemetry provides execution context that audit logs alone cannot, solving investigations faster

quotes.text: just one line, and where you place it, makes a big difference
quotes.why_it_matters: Demonstrates how code placement of validation logic directly impacts whether temporary or real data gets deleted
